title: Don't Let AI Feed You Bad Information
author: Artur Henriques
summary: Artur Henriques argues that as AI-generated documentation floods decision-making processes, the real danger isn't the AI itself but the erosion of human agency and review that accompanies it. His central claim is uncompromising: 'AI doesn't replace agency,' meaning that whoever submits an AI-assisted report for a decision is fully responsible for its contents, exactly as if they had written every word themselves, and blaming a hallucinating model for errors is 'the same as saying the author didn't even bother to read their own report carefully.' He identifies specific tells of unreviewed AI output — wildly imprecise cost estimates ('5 to 10 days' framed as an estimate rather than a guess) and missing quality-assurance validation — that decision-makers routinely wave through because 'very few people carefully read' what AI actually produced. Henriques proposes a concrete verification technique for managers: asking someone to give a two-minute spoken summary or insight on a report they submitted, arguing that 'if an engineer cannot defend a document in two minutes without reading it, they didn't write it.' The piece ends on a sharp reframe of professional negligence for the AI era: 'signing your name to an unverified LLM output is not an efficiency hack. It is negligence,' because bad decisions ultimately trace back to bad underlying assumptions nobody bothered to audit.
points: Henriques's core accountability rule — that using AI to produce a report is the same as saying, 'I built this report' — closes the responsibility loophole leaders often unconsciously grant themselves when work is AI-assisted rather than hand-written.

The two-minute defense test (asking someone to explain their AI-assisted report's conclusions aloud without notes) gives managers a lightweight, immediately usable verification technique that doesn't require auditing every underlying calculation.

Reframing unverified AI use in executive decisions as 'not an efficiency hack. It is negligence' elevates the stakes of the argument from a productivity tip to a professional-responsibility standard, directly relevant to any leader relying on AI-assisted analysis.
quotes: We cannot take AI output at face value. Someone needs to review the results and go into the weeds to determine if the assessment was done correctly.
cost estimations with 100% variation (saying that a task is done in 5 to 10 days. This is not an estimation, is a wild guess without proper foundations)
If someone uses AI to produce a report and sends it to me for decision-making, it is the same as saying, "I built this report".
Saying that Claude or ChatGPT hallucinated, or didn't consider X or Y, is the same as saying the author didn't even bother to read their own report carefully.
If an engineer cannot defend a document in two minutes without reading it, they didn't write it. This behavior should not be allowed in the company.
If someone didn't independently audit the underlying assumptions, that person didn't write an assessment: They ran a prompt.
In an executive decision, signing your name to an unverified LLM output is not an efficiency hack. It is negligence.
